items.prompt:
Read the passage below.

When most people picture a honeybee, they imagine a single insect buzzing from flower to flower. But the real marvel of the honeybee is the colony, which behaves almost like one large organism. A single hive can hold up to 60,000 bees, each with a specific job. The queen lays eggs, the workers gather nectar and build honeycomb, and the drones mate with the queen. None of these bees could survive alone for long. What makes the colony so remarkable is communication. When a worker finds a rich patch of flowers, she returns to the hive and performs a 'waggle dance,' moving her body in a figure-eight pattern. The angle and length of the dance tell the other bees exactly which direction to fly and how far to travel to reach the food. In this way, thousands of bees can share information without a single spoken word, turning a crowd of insects into a coordinated team.

The author introduces the idea of the colony in the first paragraph, then elaborates on it in the second. Explain how the second paragraph builds on the first to deepen the reader's understanding of the colony.
items.answer: The first paragraph introduces the colony as a group that acts 'almost like one large organism,' describing the different jobs bees perform and stating that none could survive alone. The second paragraph builds on this by explaining HOW the colony works so well together: through the waggle dance, which lets bees share the exact direction and distance to food. The second paragraph deepens the reader's understanding by moving from the general claim that the colony is unified to a specific illustration of the communication that makes that unity possible, turning 'a crowd of insects into a coordinated team.'

steps: Identify the key idea introduced in the first paragraph: the honeybee colony acts like one organism, with each bee doing a specific job.
Note that the first paragraph states the colony is coordinated but does not yet explain what makes the coordination possible.
Read the second paragraph and identify its new information: the waggle dance and how it communicates direction and distance.
Connect the two parts: the second paragraph explains the mechanism (communication) behind the claim made in the first (the colony acts as one).
Conclude that the second paragraph elaborates on the first by deepening the reader's understanding from a general claim to a specific, concrete example.

items.prompt:
Read the passage below.

For centuries, sailors feared a stretch of the Atlantic Ocean known as the Sargasso Sea, where thick mats of golden-brown seaweed float on the surface. Old legends claimed that ships could become tangled in the weed and trapped forever. In truth, the seaweed, called sargassum, is harmless to ships, but it is far from useless. Scientists now understand that these floating forests are nurseries teeming with life. Young sea turtles drift among the weeds, hiding from predators. Tiny crabs, shrimp, and fish found nowhere else on Earth make their homes in the tangled strands. Eels travel thousands of miles to lay their eggs in these waters. Far from being a graveyard for ships, the Sargasso Sea is one of the ocean's richest cradles of life, a floating habitat that supports creatures from their earliest days.

What is the main purpose of the second half of the passage (beginning with 'Scientists now understand')?
items.answer: The main purpose of the second half is to elaborate on the Sargasso Sea by correcting the legend introduced at the start and replacing it with a fuller, evidence-based picture. After the opening introduces the sea through old sailors' fears, the second half develops the true subject by illustrating it with specific examples: sea turtles hiding in the weeds, crabs and fish found nowhere else, and eels traveling to lay eggs. These examples build the reader's understanding that the Sargasso Sea is a 'cradle of life' rather than a graveyard, deepening and overturning the impression created by the introduction.

steps: Identify the subject: the Sargasso Sea and its floating seaweed.
Note how the introduction frames it through frightening legends about trapped ships.
Read the second half and recognize its function: it presents scientific facts and specific examples of life in the seaweed.
See that these examples (turtles, crabs, fish, eels) illustrate and elaborate the true nature of the sea.
Conclude that the second half's purpose is to develop and correct the introduction, deepening understanding rather than simply repeating it.

items.prompt:
Read the passage below.

Grace Hopper was a mathematician who helped invent the way computers work today. In the 1940s, computers were enormous machines that filled entire rooms, and programming them meant flipping switches and rewiring panels by hand. Hopper believed there had to be a better way. She imagined a system in which people could write instructions in ordinary words instead of complicated number codes. Many experts told her this was impossible, but she kept working. In 1952, she created one of the first 'compilers,' a program that translates human-readable instructions into the codes a computer can follow. Her idea became the foundation for modern programming languages, which are now written in words and symbols anyone can learn. Because of Hopper's stubborn belief that computers should serve people, millions of programmers today write software using languages that grew from her work.

How does the author develop the idea of Grace Hopper's importance across the passage, from the introduction to the end?
items.answer: The author introduces Hopper as 'a mathematician who helped invent the way computers work today,' a broad claim of importance. The middle of the passage illustrates this by describing the problem she faced (computers that had to be rewired by hand), her vision (writing instructions in ordinary words), and her solution (the 1952 compiler). The end elaborates on her importance by connecting her invention to the present, explaining that modern programming languages grew from her work and that millions of programmers benefit today. The author develops the idea by moving from a general claim, to the specific invention that backs it up, to its lasting impact, so each part builds on the one before.

steps: Identify the key individual: Grace Hopper, introduced as someone who shaped modern computing.
Trace the introduction: the opening sentence states her importance directly.
Trace the illustration: the middle gives the specific problem, her vision, and the compiler she built.
Trace the elaboration: the ending links her invention to today's programming languages and programmers.
Connect the parts to show the development moves from claim to evidence to lasting impact.

items.prompt:
Read the passage below.

Volcanoes can reshape the surface of the Earth, but they also do something surprising: they create new land. When an underwater volcano erupts, hot lava meets cold seawater and hardens into rock. With each eruption, layers of rock pile higher and higher. Over thousands of years, a volcano can grow tall enough to break the ocean's surface and form an island. The Hawaiian Islands were built this way, one eruption at a time. At first, a new volcanic island is bare and lifeless, just dark rock with no soil. But over time, wind and waves break the rock into sand. Seeds carried by birds and ocean currents take root. Slowly, plants grow, animals arrive, and a living ecosystem develops on land that did not exist before. What begins as a violent eruption deep underwater can end, ages later, as a green and thriving island.

The passage describes the volcano very differently at the end than at the beginning. Explain how the author's treatment of the subject changes, and why.
items.answer: At the beginning, the author treats the volcano as a destructive, violent force, describing 'hot lava' and the power to 'reshape the surface of the Earth.' By the end, the same volcanic process is described as creative and life-giving, producing a 'green and thriving island.' The author's treatment changes from violence to creation because the passage traces a long process over time: eruptions build rock, rock becomes an island, and the island slowly gains soil, plants, and animals. The shift shows the central idea that a destructive eruption can ultimately create new life, and the change in treatment mirrors the change the land itself undergoes.

steps: Identify the subject: volcanoes, specifically underwater ones that build islands.
Examine the opening treatment: violent, destructive, reshaping the Earth.
Examine the closing treatment: creative and life-giving, a thriving island.
Identify what links the two: the long, step-by-step process of building land and gaining life.
Conclude that the author elaborates the subject so the treatment shifts from destruction to creation, reflecting the central idea.

items.prompt:
Read the passage below.

The Great Pacific Garbage Patch is not the floating island of trash that many people imagine. Instead, it is a vast region of the ocean where currents gather plastic waste, much of it broken into tiny pieces called microplastics. These pieces are spread across an area estimated to be twice the size of Texas. Because the plastic is so small and scattered, the patch is nearly invisible from the surface of the water. This invisibility is part of what makes it so dangerous. Fish and seabirds mistake the tiny plastic fragments for food and eat them. The plastic fills their stomachs without providing nutrition, and the harmful chemicals it carries pass up the food chain. Some of these chemicals can even end up in the seafood that humans eat. A problem that is hard to see, scientists warn, can be just as serious as one we can see clearly.

The passage corrects a common image of the garbage patch in its first sentence. How does the rest of the passage build on that correction to develop the central idea?
items.answer: The first sentence introduces the subject by correcting the common image of a 'floating island of trash,' explaining instead that the patch is scattered microplastics. The rest of the passage builds on this correction by illustrating why the scattered, nearly invisible nature of the plastic is dangerous: fish and seabirds eat the tiny fragments, the plastic provides no nutrition, harmful chemicals move up the food chain, and they can reach human seafood. Each detail elaborates on the opening correction, developing the central idea that an invisible problem can be just as serious as a visible one. The parts connect by turning the surprising correction into a warning supported by specific consequences.

steps: Identify the subject: the Great Pacific Garbage Patch.
Note the introduction corrects the false image of a floating island of trash.
Identify how the rest illustrates the danger of scattered microplastics with specific consequences.
Trace the connection: the invisibility introduced first becomes the basis for the danger explained later.
Conclude that the later details elaborate the opening correction into the central idea about invisible problems.

items.prompt:
Read the passage below.

Most people know Helen Keller as a woman who could neither see nor hear, but her story is really about the power of language to open the world. An illness left Keller blind and deaf before she was two years old. For years she lived in a silent, dark world, unable to share her thoughts or understand others. Everything changed when a teacher named Anne Sullivan came into her life. Sullivan spelled words into Keller's hand, letter by letter. For weeks, the lessons seemed hopeless. Then one day, as Sullivan pumped water over one of Keller's hands and spelled 'w-a-t-e-r' into the other, Keller suddenly understood that the motions stood for the cool liquid she could feel. In that moment, language unlocked everything. Keller went on to learn to read, write, and even speak, and she became a famous author and activist. Her life showed that with the right key, even a person cut off from the world could connect with it fully.

What is the function of the 'water' moment in the development of the passage's central idea?
items.answer: The 'water' moment functions as the turning point that illustrates the central idea: the power of language to open the world. The passage introduces Keller as someone trapped in a silent, dark world, then builds toward the moment when Sullivan spells 'w-a-t-e-r' into her hand and Keller realizes the motions stand for the liquid she feels. This specific anecdote illustrates the abstract idea of language unlocking everything. The author uses it to connect the earlier description of Keller's isolation with the later description of her achievements, showing exactly how language became the 'key' that let her connect with the world.

steps: Identify the central idea: language has the power to open the world.
Note how the introduction shows Keller isolated and unable to communicate.
Recognize the 'water' moment as a specific anecdote, not just a fact.
See that it illustrates the abstract idea by showing the instant language clicked.
Conclude its function: it is the turning point connecting Keller's isolation to her later achievements.

items.prompt:
Read the passage below.

At first glance, a desert seems like the worst possible place for an animal to live. Daytime temperatures can soar above 120 degrees, water is scarce, and food can be hard to find. Yet many animals not only survive in deserts, they thrive there, thanks to remarkable adaptations. The kangaroo rat, for example, never needs to drink water at all. It gets all the moisture it needs from the dry seeds it eats, and its body is so efficient that it loses almost no water in its waste. The fennec fox survives in a different way: its enormous ears release body heat, keeping it cool, and it hunts at night to avoid the scorching sun. The camel stores fat in its hump, allowing it to go for days without eating, and it can drink huge amounts of water at once when it finds a source. Each of these animals solves the desert's challenges in its own way.

The author uses three animal examples to develop the central idea. Explain how these examples work together to support that idea.
items.answer: The central idea, introduced after the opening, is that many animals thrive in deserts because of remarkable adaptations. The author develops this idea by illustrating it with three different examples: the kangaroo rat, which gets moisture from seeds and wastes almost no water; the fennec fox, whose large ears and nighttime hunting keep it cool; and the camel, which stores fat and drinks large amounts at once. These examples work together because each shows a different solution to the same set of desert challenges (heat, scarce water, and limited food). Together they prove the central idea by showing variety: thriving in the desert is not a single trick but many specialized adaptations.

steps: Identify the central idea: animals thrive in deserts because of remarkable adaptations.
List the three examples the author uses: kangaroo rat, fennec fox, and camel.
Note that each example solves the same desert problems in a different way.
Recognize that the variety of examples illustrates the breadth of the central idea.
Conclude that the examples work together to prove adaptations are diverse and effective.

items.prompt:
Read the passage below.

The printing press, invented by Johannes Gutenberg around 1440, is often called the most important invention in human history. Before the press, books had to be copied by hand, one at a time, a process that could take a scribe months or even years for a single book. Because books were so slow to produce, they were rare and expensive, and only the wealthy and powerful could own them. Gutenberg's press changed this completely. Using movable metal letters that could be arranged, inked, and pressed onto paper, the machine could produce hundreds of identical pages in the time it once took to copy a single one. Suddenly books became cheaper and more common. Ideas that had been locked away in a few libraries could now spread across whole countries. Ordinary people learned to read, new ideas challenged old authorities, and knowledge that once belonged to the few became available to the many.

How does the author use the description of book-copying before the press to develop the central idea about the printing press?
items.answer: The author introduces the printing press as possibly 'the most important invention in human history,' then develops that claim by first describing how books were made before the press: copied by hand, one at a time, taking months or years, making books rare and expensive. This description illustrates the problem the press solved. By contrasting the slow, costly hand-copying with the press's ability to make hundreds of identical pages quickly, the author shows exactly why the invention mattered. The 'before' description connects to the 'after' description to elaborate the central idea that the printing press spread knowledge from the few to the many.

steps: Identify the central idea: the printing press was a hugely important invention because it spread knowledge.
Note the introduction makes a strong claim about the press's importance.
See that the 'before' description (hand-copying) sets up the problem the press solved.
Recognize the contrast between slow hand-copying and fast printing develops the idea.
Conclude that the 'before' details connect to the 'after' details to show why the press mattered.

items.prompt:
Read the passage below.

For a long time, scientists believed that crows and other members of the crow family were simply ordinary birds. Recent research has shown that this view was badly mistaken. Crows are among the smartest animals on the planet. In one famous experiment, a crow was given a short stick that could not reach a piece of food, along with a long stick locked inside a box. The crow used the short stick to free the long stick, then used the long stick to reach the food, solving a multi-step problem that few animals can manage. Crows also recognize individual human faces and can remember a person who treated them badly for years. In cities, some crows have learned to drop hard nuts onto crosswalks so that passing cars crack the shells, then wait for the traffic light to turn red before safely collecting the food. These behaviors reveal a kind of intelligence once thought to belong only to humans and a few other mammals.

Identify which example in the passage best illustrates that crows can plan ahead, and explain how it develops the central idea.
items.answer: The example that best illustrates crows planning ahead is the city crows that drop hard nuts onto crosswalks so passing cars crack the shells, then wait for the red light before collecting the food. This develops the central idea that crows are among the smartest animals because it shows them combining several steps toward a goal and timing their actions for safety, which requires planning and foresight. The author introduces the central idea (crows are highly intelligent), then illustrates it with examples of increasing sophistication, and this crosswalk example deepens the idea by showing intelligence that looks deliberate and forward-thinking, not just clever in the moment.

steps: Identify the central idea: crows are among the smartest animals.
Review the examples: the stick experiment, recognizing faces, and the crosswalk nut-dropping.
Determine which shows planning ahead: the crosswalk example, where crows time actions and use traffic.
Explain how it shows foresight: combining steps and waiting for a safe moment.
Connect it to the central idea by showing it deepens the proof of crow intelligence.

items.prompt:
Read the passage below.

The Amazon rainforest is sometimes called 'the lungs of the Earth,' and the nickname captures an important truth. Stretching across nine countries in South America, the Amazon is the largest tropical rainforest in the world. Its billions of trees take in carbon dioxide and release oxygen, helping to keep the air breathable for living things across the globe. But the Amazon's importance goes far beyond the air. The forest is home to one in ten of all known species on the planet, including jaguars, pink river dolphins, and thousands of kinds of frogs, birds, and insects found nowhere else. The Amazon also stores enormous amounts of water and helps create rainfall that waters farmland far away. When large areas of the forest are cut down, the effects ripple outward, harming the climate, wiping out species, and changing weather patterns thousands of miles away.

The passage opens with the nickname 'the lungs of the Earth.' Explain how the rest of the passage both supports and goes beyond that nickname to develop the central idea.
items.answer: The passage introduces the Amazon with the nickname 'the lungs of the Earth,' which highlights how the forest's trees take in carbon dioxide and release oxygen. The passage supports this nickname by explaining that the billions of trees keep the air breathable across the globe. But the author then goes beyond the nickname to develop a fuller central idea: the Amazon also shelters one in ten known species, stores huge amounts of water, and creates rainfall for distant farmland. By moving from the air to biodiversity to water and weather, the author elaborates the subject, showing that the Amazon's importance is broader than the single image of 'lungs' suggests, and that harming it causes wide-ranging effects.

steps: Identify the introduction: the nickname 'lungs of the Earth' and its meaning about oxygen.
Note how the passage first supports the nickname by explaining the trees' role in the air.
Identify the move beyond the nickname: biodiversity, water storage, and rainfall.
Recognize that these added details elaborate the subject past the single image.
Conclude the central idea is the Amazon's broad, far-reaching importance.

items.prompt:
Read the passage below.

Most of us think of bones as hard, dead scaffolding inside the body, but bones are actually living, changing tissue. A bone is constantly being broken down and rebuilt by special cells. One type of cell dissolves old bone, while another type lays down fresh bone in its place. This is why a broken bone can heal: the body simply rebuilds the damaged area. The process also explains why exercise strengthens bones. When you run, jump, or lift, you put stress on your bones, and the body responds by building them thicker and stronger to handle the load. The opposite is also true. Astronauts who spend months in space, where there is little gravity to push against, lose bone mass because their bones are no longer being challenged. Far from being lifeless, your skeleton is a busy construction site that responds to how you live.

How does the information about astronauts in space help develop the central idea of the passage?
items.answer: The central idea is that bones are living, changing tissue that respond to how the body is used. The author introduces this idea, illustrates it with the way bones heal and grow stronger with exercise, and then uses the astronaut example to develop it further by showing the opposite case. Because astronauts in space have little gravity to push against, their bones are not challenged and lose mass. This example deepens the central idea by proving the point from the other direction: just as stress builds bone, the absence of stress weakens it. The astronaut detail connects to the earlier exercise example to show that bones constantly respond to the demands placed on them.

steps: Identify the central idea: bones are living tissue that respond to how the body is used.
Note the illustration that exercise and stress make bones stronger.
Recognize the astronaut example shows the opposite: no stress means bone loss.
See that this opposite case develops the idea by proving it from another angle.
Conclude the astronaut detail connects to the exercise detail to deepen the central idea.

items.prompt:
Read the passage below.

Wangari Maathai grew up in the highlands of Kenya, surrounded by green forests and clear streams. When she returned home as an adult after studying abroad, she was alarmed by what she saw. Many of the forests had been cut down, the streams had dried up, and the soil was washing away. Women had to walk farther and farther to find firewood and clean water. Maathai realized that the loss of trees was at the heart of these problems. In 1977, she began an organization called the Green Belt Movement, encouraging ordinary women to plant trees in their own communities. At first the idea seemed small, but it grew. Over the years, the movement planted more than fifty million trees across Kenya and inspired similar efforts in other African countries. By connecting the health of the land to the well-being of people, Maathai showed that even a single tree could be a powerful act of change. In 2004, she became the first African woman to win the Nobel Peace Prize.

Trace how the author develops the idea of Maathai's accomplishment from the beginning of the passage to the end.
items.answer: The author introduces Maathai through her childhood in a green, healthy Kenyan landscape, then shows her return as an adult to find forests cut down, streams dried up, and soil eroding. This sets up the problem. The middle of the passage illustrates her response: realizing trees were central to the problem and founding the Green Belt Movement in 1977 to get women planting trees. The author then elaborates on her accomplishment by tracing the movement's growth, from a small idea to more than fifty million trees planted and similar efforts across Africa. The ending deepens the idea by naming her Nobel Peace Prize. The development moves from the problem, to her solution, to its growing impact, to lasting recognition, with each part building on the one before.

steps: Identify the key individual: Wangari Maathai and her environmental work.
Trace the introduction: her green childhood and the damaged landscape she returns to.
Trace the illustration: she founds the Green Belt Movement and women plant trees.
Trace the elaboration: the movement grows to fifty million trees and spreads.
Note the ending (Nobel Prize) and connect the stages to show the building development.

items.prompt:
Read the passage below.

For years, doctors gave patients strict advice: if you have a back injury or sore muscles, rest in bed until you feel better. It seemed like common sense. If something hurts, stop using it. But modern research has turned this advice upside down. Studies now show that staying in bed too long can actually make many injuries worse. When muscles are not used, they grow weak, joints stiffen, and recovery slows down. For most common back pain, doctors now recommend gentle movement, such as short walks, rather than long bed rest. Movement increases blood flow to the injured area, which carries the nutrients the body needs to heal. It also keeps muscles strong enough to support the spine. The old advice was not entirely wrong, since serious injuries do require rest, but for everyday aches and strains, the body often heals faster when it keeps moving.

The passage develops its central idea by contrasting old advice with new research. Explain how this contrast helps the reader understand the central idea.
items.answer: The passage introduces the subject with the old advice to rest in bed after an injury, calling it common sense. It then develops the central idea by contrasting that advice with modern research showing that too much rest can make injuries worse, while gentle movement speeds healing by increasing blood flow and keeping muscles strong. This contrast helps the reader understand the central idea because it shows clearly what changed and why: the new view is not just a different opinion but a correction based on evidence. By setting the surprising old advice against the new findings, the author makes the central idea, that movement often heals everyday injuries better than rest, easier to grasp and more convincing.

steps: Identify the central idea: gentle movement often heals everyday injuries better than long bed rest.
Note the introduction presents the old advice to rest in bed.
Identify the contrast: modern research shows rest can worsen injuries and movement helps.
Explain how the contrast shows what changed and why, using evidence.
Conclude the contrast makes the central idea clearer and more convincing.

items.prompt:
Read the passage below.

The word 'robot' did not come from a scientist or an engineer. It came from a play. In 1920, a Czech writer named Karel Capek wrote a drama about artificial workers built to serve humans. He needed a name for these creatures, and his brother suggested the word 'robota,' a Czech term meaning forced labor. The shortened form, 'robot,' stuck, and the play became famous around the world. At first, robots existed only in stories and imagination. Decades later, though, real machines began to match the idea. By the 1960s, the first industrial robots were welding car parts on factory assembly lines. Today, robots explore the deep ocean, perform delicate surgery, and even roll across the surface of Mars. The word that began as a made-up term in a single play now describes machines that do work once thought impossible, just as Capek imagined, though in ways he could never have predicted.

What is the function of the final sentence in the development of the passage's central idea?
items.answer: The final sentence functions as a conclusion that connects the beginning of the passage to the end and synthesizes the central idea: the word 'robot' began as an invented term in a single play and now describes real machines doing once-impossible work. The passage introduces the surprising origin of the word in Capek's 1920 play, then illustrates the rise of real robots from factory assembly lines to surgery and Mars exploration. The final sentence elaborates by linking the imaginary origin to the modern reality, noting that robots do work Capek imagined 'though in ways he could never have predicted.' It ties the parts together, showing how a made-up word grew into a description of real technology.

steps: Identify the central idea: a made-up word from a play became the name for real, powerful machines.
Note the introduction: the word's origin in Capek's 1920 play.
Note the illustration: real robots from assembly lines to surgery to Mars.
Recognize the final sentence links the imaginary origin to the modern reality.
Conclude its function: it concludes and synthesizes the central idea by connecting beginning and end.

items.prompt:
Read the passage below.

When a wildfire sweeps through a forest, it looks like total destruction. Blackened trees, gray ash, and silence replace the green and busy woodland that stood before. For a long time, people believed that all forest fires were disasters to be prevented at any cost. Yet scientists have learned that many forests actually depend on fire to stay healthy. Some pine trees, for example, have cones sealed shut with a thick resin. Only the intense heat of a fire can melt the resin and release the seeds inside, allowing new trees to sprout. Fire also clears away dead branches and thick underbrush that would otherwise pile up and choke young plants. After a fire, sunlight reaches the forest floor, and the ash left behind enriches the soil with nutrients. Within a few years, fresh green growth returns, often stronger than before. What looks at first like an ending is, for these forests, a kind of beginning.

The passage develops the idea that fire can help forests. Explain how the examples in the middle of the passage connect the frightening opening image to the hopeful closing image.
items.answer: The passage opens with a frightening image of a forest after a wildfire: blackened trees, ash, and silence, reflecting the old belief that all fires are disasters. It closes with a hopeful image of fresh green growth that returns 'often stronger than before.' The examples in the middle connect these two images by explaining how fire actually helps: the heat melts resin so pine cones release their seeds, fire clears dead underbrush that would choke young plants, and ash enriches the soil. These examples illustrate the central idea and bridge the opening and closing, showing the reader the process that turns apparent destruction into renewal, so that 'what looks at first like an ending is a kind of beginning.'

steps: Identify the central idea: many forests depend on fire to stay healthy.
Note the frightening opening image of destruction after a fire.
Note the hopeful closing image of stronger new growth.
Identify the middle examples: melting resin releases seeds, fire clears underbrush, ash enriches soil.
Explain that these examples connect the opening to the closing by showing how destruction leads to renewal.
